source.title: Quantization-Robust Unlearning through the Lens of Retain-Forget Loss Landscapes Interaction
source.authors: Jia-Lu Wang; Jia-Ning Deng; Shu-Qing Luo; Yuan-Zhe Li; Dong-Wei Wang; Jing-Tong Hu; Huan-Rui Yang; Song Wang; Tian-Long Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether post-training quantization restores forgotten knowledge, and whether quantization-aware unlearning reduces that effect.
record.gate_note: The study reports forgetting and retained-knowledge metrics before and after quantization. Its loss-landscape analysis describes quantization sensitivity, but does not test activation-direction ablation or establish that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge. Table 1's flattened multi-group layout is not used for separately attributed numerical rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures forget-set KnowMem before and after 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) on MUSE, which bears directly on D and on A's 'simple attacks don't recover' clause. It also tests counter-methods (SURE, the paper's regularization, and its full framework) against quantization recovery, which bears on F. It is not one of the original sources. B, C and E are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that 4-bit post-training quantization substantially undoes forgetting because unlearned solutions sit in sharp forget-loss basins. Their sensitivity-guided noisy regularization plus forget-critical layer updates gives substantially more quantization-robust forgetting with comparable utility. The quantization experiments are on MUSE only; TOFU results concern the forget–utility trade-off of layer selection, not quantization.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates post-training quantization after GA, NPO, and other unlearning objectives, and proposes quantization-aware unlearning; it does not test fine-tuning, activation ablation, or prompt attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with unlearning objective, dataset, quantization method, and whether SURE or the proposed regularization is used. The authors also report that the parameter-selection ratio affects the forgetting–utility trade-off.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss-landscape visualizations (Fig. 2, Fig. 4) show the forget-loss basin is much sharper than the retain-loss basin after standard unlearning. The authors trace quantization fragility to this sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard unlearning converges to sharp forget-loss minima, so small weight perturbations reintroduce forgotten behavior.

record.problems: No error bars or uncertainty estimates are reported in the presented results. The displayed results focus on 4-bit quantization; 8-bit behavior is characterized as close to full precision based on cited prior work. The paper reports limited model and benchmark coverage for the quantization experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 is not separately extracted because the flattened multi-method layout does not unambiguously align all metrics and settings in the supplied text. Tables 4 and 5 report parameter-selection-ratio variants; they are omitted because the main quantization comparisons and generalization results are represented above. Table 2's VerbMem and Knowr metrics are not duplicated where the extracted KnowMem result already captures the forget-set recovery or utility comparison.

untested.parts: Near-chance targeted accuracy is not assessed; MUSE uses retrain or target references. Fine-tuning, activation-edit and prompting attacks are not tested.
Entirely untested. The loss-landscape analysis is not an ablation or access-vs-deletion test.
8-bit and other bit-widths are not run; 8-bit is described only from prior work. TOFU and Llama-3 models are not evaluated under quantization.
Resistance to fine-tuning relearning, activation ablation and prompting attacks is not tested. Only quantization is tested, and only on MUSE with two 7B models.

missing.what: Table 1 is parseable and contains the full framework (+Ours) and SURE vs 4-bit for GA/NPO × NoReg/KLR/GDR on MUSE-News. Examples: GA-GDR 28.9→50.1 (4-bit), 34.6 (SURE), 28.3 (Ours); NPO-GDR 46.1→51.4, 35.9, 34.3; NPO-NoReg 0→25.4 under 4-bit; GA-KLR Ours 33.0 vs FP 27.1.

VerbMem on the forget set before and after quantization, which shows large verbatim recovery. Examples: Books GAKLR 13.0→75.6, NPOKLR 12.4→70.9; News NPOGDR 0.3→29.4/30.1. Under the defenses VerbMem stays well above FP (21-26 vs 0.3-14.1).
Quantized target and retrain reference values (Books target 4-bit Know 36.8; News 54.4; retrain 24.1/36.0). These are needed to judge how complete the recovery is.

record.verdict_notes: Defended-condition rows were moved from D/A to F, and their states re-judged as resistance relative to FP and undefended 4-bit values; the reader had judged them against D. The in-text '13%→54%' average is inconsistent with Table 2 ratios. NPOGDR's FP KnowMem (46.1) already exceeds retrain (33.1), so FP unlearning of knowledge was itself weak there. Quantization also restores utility in collapsed NoReg models, which complicates reading forget-metric rises as recovery alone. No uncertainty estimates are reported. SURE is a prior method (Zhang et al. 2024b), tested here as a comparator.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports forgetting and utility metrics but does not establish that targeted accuracy is near chance across conditions or test prompting, fine-tuning, and activation-edit attacks.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation is tested, and the analysis does not test whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
The reported experiments focus on 4-bit post-training quantization; 8-bit results are described only as close to full precision based on prior work.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context prompting attack is tested.
The proposed method is tested against quantization, not against fine-tuning, activation edits, or prompting attacks.

The Section 3 average (13% to 54%) can't be reproduced from Table 1.

statements.problem: Minor naming only: the text calls its main 4-bit quantizer bitsandbytes and defines it as round-to-nearest (Eq. 2); it never uses the word RTN.

statements.correction: NPOGDR MUSE-News (LLaMA2-7B): KnowMem 46.1 to 49.6 (AWQ) and 48.9 (GPTQ); VerbMem 0.3 to 29.4 and 30.1; quantized-target VerbMem 34.2 (Tables 2, 3).
statements.problem: Puts this study's NPOGDR cells in an entry saying quantization 'adds little'. But VerbMem rises 0.3 to 29.4/30.1 there, and the record's verdict is limits_scope, not challenges.
Minor naming only: the text calls the 50.9 quantizer bitsandbytes (defined as round-to-nearest, Eq. 2), not RTN by name.

statements.correction: GAKLR MUSE-News KnowMem: FP 27.1; AWQ 49.8, with method 36.9; GPTQ 49.3, with method 37.9 (Table 3). SURE NPOKLR Books: 36.9, against 34.2 undefended and 13.7 FP.
statements.problem: Lists the full method's AWQ/GPTQ values as challenge evidence but leaves out the undefended 49.8/49.3. The method roughly halves recovery, and the record's verdict for these cells is limits_scope (l4).

statements.correction: Main 4-bit quantizer is bitsandbytes (Eq. 2 rounding); AWQ/GPTQ only in Table 3, News. Undefended values: r2 34.6 vs 15.1, r3 34.2 vs 13.7, r4 50.9 vs 27.1.
statements.problem: Says the Table 2 quantizer is not stated, but the text states bitsandbytes for the main experiments. The cited rows r7, r9, r10 hold other values; the numbers quoted are r2, r3 and r4.
Cites r15, r17 but makes no claim about this study.
36.9 (SURE NPOKLR Books, r8) is right; 4.8 GA_GDR is not from this study; r12 is cited but not described.

statements.correction: Books NPOKLR KnowMem: FP 13.7, 4-bit 34.2, 4-bit+SURE 36.9 (Table 2). The text credits SURE to Zhang et al. 2024b (2410.16454) and never says SURE was rerun.
statements.problem: Counts r8 as an outside group breaking SURE. But 36.9 vs 34.2 equals SURE's own paper (2410.16454) as reported in this pack, and D.suggested_status treats this study as repeating 2410.16454's values.
